9bf44e7706318565: Learning in a room changes what you notice
6c523b6e5d507379: Some things are hard to teach through a screen. One of them is the hydrometer. Most read true at 20 °C (68 °F), so a sample read hot gives a low number and a wrong ABV. In a room we put the jar in your hand, take a reading hot, cool the sample and read it again, so you see the error yourself.
c72a77255e9c282c: The same goes for smelling a crushed malt next to a whole one or feeling how sticky a sanitised surface is not. These are small moments. They are the reason this bundle is taught in person.
3ae810525342a918: Sanitation is the other lesson that lands better in person. A no-rinse sanitiser needs the right dilution and contact time to work. A fermenter that looks clean can still carry a film of soil that sanitiser cannot get through. Cleaning comes first and sanitising second. Seeing a brewer do both in order, then doing it yourself, is how the habit forms before your first batch at home.

10d4ccb1dde440c4: Every brewing book tells you to mash at around 65 °C (149 °F). Few tell you that strike water has to go in several degrees hotter, because cold malt and a cold vessel pull the temperature down the moment they meet. Stand at a mash tun once, watch the thermometer drop and you will never forget it.

9f44b50aca42bc12: Brewing in Indian heat is part of the syllabus
83e41335f7e78103: A recipe written for a cool climate assumes a cool room. In Pune, Delhi, Gurugram and Bengaluru, a garage or kitchen can sit above 30 °C (86 °F) for months, which is ten degrees or more over the 18 to 20 °C (64 to 68 °F) most ale yeasts want. Warm fermentation throws fruity esters and harsh fusel alcohols. It is one of the most common faults in first beers brewed in Indian heat.
1b4938ba6ba83413: So both courses spend time on control: how a glycol-jacketed fermenter holds temperature in a brewery, plus what a homebrewer can do with a fridge, a controller or a heat-tolerant yeast such as kveik. Our guide to brewing for India goes further.
